ARTICLE IN PRESS The impact of work–family equilibrium on employee proactive behaviors Abstract: This study examined 126 companies, collecting valid data from 1,354 employees and 142 human resource managers. Polynomial regression and response surface analysis methods were employed to explore the differentiated influence of the equilibrium states of work–family conflict and work–family facilitation on employees' proactive behaviors based on the resource conservation theory. The study found that work–family conflict and facilitation have a significant direct impact on employees' proactive behavior. The degree of equilibrium between work–family conflict and work– S family facilitation has a significant impact on employees' proactive behavior. Emotional S E exhaustion and psychological capital played mediating roles in the influence of the R work–family equilibrium state on employee proactive behavior. This study enriches the P research on the antecedent variables of employees’ proactive behaviors and the outcome N variables of work–family integration, oIffering theoretical recommendations for future E research and human resource management practices. Introduction In pursuing the enhancement of national economic competitiveness, it is critical to cultivate and strengthen core competitiveness and capabilities of corporations. These topics have accordingly become major focuses of extensive research. As key drivers of high-quality development, enterprises that can factually enhance their core competitiveness are attracting significant societal attention. Meanwhile, in the modern- day context of a complex, volatile, and fiercely-competitive environment, enterprise development is extensively reliant relies on employees' collective efforts. Indeed, employee proactive behavior (PB) enhances work efficiency and performance, organizational operational efficiency, enterprise competitiveness, and reduces S management costs (Fu et al., 2020). This makes efforts to foster such behaviors a main S challenge for organizations. E R Importantly, employee behaviors are embedded within organizational contexts, P where structural and social factors significantly shape attitudes and actions. Many prior N studies delving into the antecedent variables of employees' PBs have focused on I individual and organizational factors (Han et al., 2023). Others have substantially E investigated family-work dynamics, and yet relatively few have examined how family L factors in social situations inCteract with typical work relationships taking place across I family and organizational contexts to influence employees’ PBs. In examining this T specific gap, this stRudy theoretically complements the literature on antecedents of A employee PB. In current times, there is an ongoing restructuring of the workforce, with employees increasingly pursuing holistic well-being alongside professional fulfillment. Family well-being, a main dimension of life satisfaction, significantly shapes employee behavior (Han, 2023). Work and family constitute dynamically-interacting, interdependent life domains within employees’ lived experiences (Deng et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2007), and there is both conflict and facilitatory processes to be found amid work–family relationships (Brummelhuis & Bakker, 2012). While extant research examines how these constructs independently affect work attitudes and behaviors (Wang et al., 2022), their interactive dynamics—particularly how their equilibrium influences PBs—remain underexplored. Since work–family conflict (WFC) and facilitation (WFF) coexist as non-mutually exclusive forces (e.g., overtime work may strain family life while enhancing familial resources through compensation), their ARTICLE IN PRESS relative intensity may determine whether these opposing dynamics reach equilibrium. This constitutes a major but understudied mediator of employee outcomes. Accordingly, this study examined how organizations manage WFC and WFF through human resources (HR) practices. Integrating both constructs within a conservation of resources (COR) framework, we employ polynomial regression with response surface analysis (RSA) to investigate how work–family equilibrium (high/low) versus disequilibrium differentially predicts employee PB. Boundary conditions moderating these effects are further analyzed. The study offers three main contributions. First, theoretical advancement through COR-based integration of the WFC–WFF duality. Second, empirical innovation via testing equilibrium-disequilibrium continua. Third, innovative leadership through S pioneering RSA applications in work–family research. Employees simultaneously experience WFC and WFF as these coexist dynamically (Chen et al., 2014), both exerting significant psychological and behavioral S impacts (Frone et al., 1992). Emotional exhaustion and even aggressive behaviors may occur when employees experience WFC. Meanwhile, PB requires employees to invest in a certain degree of cognition, emotion, energy, and other resources (Zhang et al., 2018). Other studies have confirmed that WFF can effectively reduce emotional exhaustion. (Liu et al., 2019) showed that psychological capital elements (e.g., optimism and hope) were effective predictive S variables of job burnout. (Shi, 2019) examined the impaSct of emotional exhaustion on E CWB through a moderating analysis of psychological capital, finding that R psychological capital directly and effectively reduces emotional exhaustion. On the one hand, WFC brings N about great increases in employees' emotional exhaustion; on the other, WFF I continuously reduces the occurrence o f such exhaustion. From the perspective R of resource loss and gain, positive emotions are important resources for employees. A When emotional resources are consumed to a certain extent, self-restraining ability is reduced. That is, employees become less capable of restraining their behaviors and fulfill the requirements of their roles (Baumeister et al., 1998). Resource conservation theory shows that negative emotional reactions will lead to depressed work attitude and decreased work enthusiasm, which could lead to job burnout and even induce turnover intention (Oh et al., 2024). In short, in a high– high equilibrium, employees’ emotional exhaustion will be at a high level. At the same time, when there is a low–low equilibrium, employees’ emotional S exhaustion is low. Conclusions and implications 5.1 Main Conclusions WWC and WWF have important direct impacts on employee PB. Based on resource protection theory, this study analyzed the mechanism of WFC-WFF S equilibrium on employee PB, exploring the mediating effects of emotional exhaustion S and psychological capital. E First, the WFC–WFF equilibrium had an imRportant direct impact on PB, with a curvilinear relationship. Considering a WFC–WPFF equilibrium, PB is higher when the match is high–high than when low–loNw. Meanwhile, considering a WFC–WFF disequilibrium, WFC reduces PB, wheIreas the latter enhances it, and in a low–high match, the resources generated by WEFF can provide support for individuals to an extent L that is greater than the resource losses caused by WFC. Thus, individuals find C themselves in a value-addeId spiral effect that enables them to acquire more resources T and pursue PBs at work. R Second, emAotional exhaustion and psychological capital played a mediating role on the association of WFC–WFF equilibrium state with PB. Additionally, different equilibrium states significantly impacted both emotional exhaustion and psychological capital. WFC had a significantly positive impact on emotional exhaustion and a significantly negative impact on psychological capital, while WFF had a significantly positive effect on psychological capital and a negative effect on emotional exhaustion. Emotional exhaustion partially mediated the effects of WFC–WFF equilibrium state on PB, while psychological capital provided full mediation. 5.2 Major contributions First, this research expands the theoretical perspective on PB by investigating its antecedents, thereby providing a novel theoretical window for organizations to stimulate such behavior. ARTICLE IN PRESS Second, by examining WFC and WFF within an integrated framework, this study investigated the impact of their equilibrium on employee PB, offering greater alignment with real-world contexts and enriching the theoretical discourse on work–family relationships. In practice, employees experience both WFC and WFF simultaneously, albeit existing research have predominantly focused on their separate effects on work attitudes, behaviors, and organizational outcomes. Meanwhile, the simultaneous presence of WFC and WFF often creates imbalanced states for employees. Grounded in conservation of resources theory, this study employed polynomial regression and RSA to empirically validate its theoretical framework. The findings support the proposed hypotheses, contributing to the literature by diversifying the outcome variables in work-family research and offering a new S exploratory perspective for future studies in this field. S E 5.3 Management implications R P The confirmation of the influence of different WFC–WFF equilibrium states on PB is conducive to enterprises formulaNting corresponding management strategies I according to employees’ individual situations regarding conflict and facilitators. To E ensure that employees engage in PB at work and ultimately create competitive L advantages for enterprises, we suggest the following human resource management C practices. I T First, building a harmonious work-family relationship; for employees, work– R family balance siAgnificantly impacts PB. WFC had a significant negative impact on PB, entailing that enterprises should adopt targeted human resource management practices to help employees cope with the negative impacts of such conflict. There should be efforts to improve employees’ work autonomy, create flexible work schemes, good work opportunities and conditions, and encouragement for the completion of work tasks according to their own needs and the actual job situation. Enterprises should fully consider the characteristics of employees and check whether they should adopt flexible working methods such as working from home, job sharing, and flexible leave to optimize work–family balance. Second, implementing a psychological capital development plan for employees. Our findings show that psychological capital significantly positively influences PB. Enterprises should thus make full use of psychological capital to increase PB; like human capital, psychological capital can be developed and improved. Enterprises can ARTICLE IN PRESS develop plans based on the four core elements of psychological capital, including work enrichment and expansion. Efforts to create a loose and inclusive organizational culture may increase employees’ experiences of joy and self-confidence. Enterprises can also develop a positive team atmosphere and corporate culture, strengthen employees’ psychological counseling, and cultivate optimistic attitudes within the organization. Organizations should also pay attention to employees’ emotional states and provide more organizational care to employees with emotional exhaustion. Psychological capital development plans for employees can play a significant role for talent development in enterprises and positively impact employees’ lives. Third, reducing negative emotions. Emotional exhaustion had a significantly negative impact on PB. Therefore, enterprises can implement effective employee S assistance programs to try and reduce employees’ negative psychological states, WFCs, S and improve passion for work and life satisfaction. Measures such as psychological E interventions, efforts to provide proper medical diaRgnosis and treatment for employees, stress prevention training, self-recognition trainPing, and case analysis to guide and help employees resolve and relieve negative Nemotions can all enhance positive working emotions, help employees find joy andI meaning in work, and improve their sense of E accomplishment and happiness at work. L C 5.4 Research limitations aInd prospects T This study alsoR has several limitations. First, while it focused on the impact of work–family relaAtionships at the individual level on employee PB, other organizational factors such as organizational culture, leadership style, and human resource policies may also significantly influence PB. Second, the control variables included in the study mainly consist of gender, age, education level, organizational tenure, and marital status, while factors related to children in the family were not considered. Previous research has shown that in the Chinese context, family childrearing circumstances significantly affect work–family relationships and employee work behavior (Li et al., 2024). In particular, grandparenting in China’s specific sociocultural background can also influence employees’ work motivation (He & Wang, 2015). Therefore, future studies should incorporate examinations into the effects of children and grandparenting. Third, this study primarily used data from employees within enterprises without distinguishing between younger and older groups. Research indicates that these two ARTICLE IN PRESS groups prioritize work and family differently, warranting future comparative analyses across different demographic segments. Fourth, most measurement tools adopted in this study originated from international literature. Although the scales demonstrated good reliability and validity, their applicability in the Chinese context remains debatable. Future research could localize and optimize these measurement tools based on China’s specific context to ensure that they are optimally aligned with the practices of Chinese enterprises. JSON: Name: work_family_equilibrium_proactivity Title: Polynomial regression and response surface analysis of work–family equilibrium effects on employee proactive behavior Short Hypothesis: Employees in configurations where work–family facilitation exceeds work–family conflict will exhibit higher levels of proactive behavior than employees in configurations where work–family conflict exceeds facilitation. Related Work: Prior research has evaluated work–family conflict (WFC) and work–family facilitation (WFF) largely as separate, linear antecedents of work outcomes using additive regression, structural equation models, or job-demands/resources frameworks. Conservation of resources (COR) and JD-R perspectives explain resource loss/gain effects on behavior but have been operationalized primarily through main effects; difference-score and interaction-term approaches have been used sporadically. Existing work has limitedly applied configuration methods (e.g., polynomial regression with response surface analysis) to model simultaneous WFC–WFF states, and few studies test nonlinear or equilibrium/disequilibrium effects. Mediator tests have typically focused on single pathways (e.g., burnout or engagement) using cross-sectional SEM and often suffer from common-method and cultural measurement validity issues. Gaps include insufficient modeling of configurational curvilinear effects, limited use of validated mediation testing for configuration predictors, inadequate multilevel controls for nested organizational data, and weak external validity across industries and cultures. Abstract: This research investigates how configurations of work–family conflict and work–family facilitation predict employee proactive behavior using polynomial regression and response surface analysis. We address whether disequilibrium (one domain dominating the other) versus equilibrium (both high or both low) produces distinct impacts on proactive behaviors, and whether emotional exhaustion and psychological capital mediate these configuration effects. The approach models WFC and WFF simultaneously as continuous predictors, estimates quadratic and product terms, and interprets slopes/curvatures along agreement and disagreement lines in the response surface; mediation is assessed via bootstrap estimates of indirect surface effects. The main contribution is an empirical pipeline that quantifies configuration-level predictors of proactive behavior and tests dual mediation pathways. Expected outcomes are (1) higher proactive behavior when facilitation exceeds conflict and (2) differential indirect effects through emotional exhaustion and psychological capital depending on equilibrium/disequilibrium. Findings will refine theoretical accounts of work–family resource dynamics and inform HR interventions. Experiments: Datasets: primary sample of cross-sectional and two-wave survey data from employees and HR managers (target n≈1,300+ employees, n≈100+ HR reps, across ~100 firms) and an independent replication sample (n≥500). Measures: validated scales for WFC (multi-item), WFF (multi-item), proactive behavior (multi-item), emotional exhaustion, and psychological capital; control covariates: gender, age, education, tenure, marital status, firm ID. Preprocessing: remove respondents reporting employer change between waves, handle missingness via listwise deletion and multiple imputation sensitivity, standardize predictors (z-scores) prior to polynomial terms, center covariates where appropriate. Baselines: (A) additive linear regression (WFC + WFF), (B) difference-score model (WFF − WFC), (C) interaction-only model (WFC*WFF), (D) polynomial regression without RSA diagnostics, (E) multilevel linear mixed model (random intercepts by firm). Primary model: polynomial regression including linear, squared, and cross-product terms for WFC and WFF; compute RSA parameters (slope and curvature along X=Y and X=−Y). Mediation tests: two-stage approach — (1) polynomial regression predicting mediators (EE and PC), (2) polynomial regression predicting PB with mediators added; estimate indirect/configurational mediation using bootstrap (n=5,000) of block-weighted indirect effects and report 95% CIs. Evaluation metrics: adjusted R^2, RMSE, AIC/BIC for model comparison; significance and effect sizes for RSA slopes/curvatures; bootstrap CI for indirect effects; proportion mediated. Ablations and robustness checks: (1) remove quadratic terms to test added value, (2) include single mediators separately and jointly, (3) substitute difference-score and interaction models, (4) run multilevel RSA-equivalent models (random slopes), (5) test measurement invariance across sectors and gender, (6) sensitivity to standardization vs. centering, (7) alternative estimators (SEM with latent variables) for measurement-error adjustment. Report all model coefficients, RSA parameter estimates, bootstrap distributions, and replicate primary analyses on replication sample. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self-report measures and survey design create common-method bias and limit causal inference despite two-wave timing; temporal precedence for mediation remains imperfect. Polynomial regression/RSA is susceptible to multicollinearity among higher-order terms and to unstable curvature estimates in small or uneven samples. Model interpretation of response surfaces can be sensitive to scaling and standardization choices. Sample representativeness may be limited by geography, industry composition, or reliance on convenience/partner firms, reducing generalizability. Measurement instruments adapted from other cultures may have construct validity issues in the study population. Mediational findings are vulnerable to omitted confounders (e.g., leadership style, organizational policies) and measurement error; bootstrap CIs do not resolve bias from unmeasured confounding. Multilevel dependence (employees nested within firms) can inflate Type I error if not modeled correctly; small numbers of firms limit random-effect estimation. Nonlinear effects detected in one context may not replicate across cultures or labor market conditions. Computationally, exhaustive bootstrap and multilevel RSA analyses increase runtime and require adequate compute resources.
